reviewer_concerns.concern_text: All children in the study underwent ECG. The authors should provide further comment on the indications for this ECG – I assume that an ECG is not performed routinely (i.e., among patients in whom CHD is not suspected), and therefore the presence of an ECG for clinical purposes is subject to indication bias. This is a substantial limitation since it becomes unclear how the model would perform when applied prospectively among individuals who would not necessarily otherwise get an ECG (such as those who could be 'screened' for CHD as the authors suggest as a primary use case).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the indication bias, removed 'CHD screening' claims, and added a limitation noting the cohort came from a real-world referral context, not from screening of general pediatric population.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clarification of phenotyping is needed. Specifically, reference is made to CHD detection 'following the standard guideline with various tools', but no reference or guidelines are provided, and the description is vague. A clearer definition of how each CHD was defined would be useful.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that diagnostic workup followed the ESC Guidelines for CHD (primarily transthoracic echocardiography + ECG), cited the 2020 ESC guideline reference, and clarified attending-physician final adjudication.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Is there any assessment of model calibration? How accurate are the predicted probabilities on an absolute basis? This is a fundamental component of model evaluation that appears lacking.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Brier score as a calibration measure to Table 1; reported values close to 0 indicating good calibration. They added explanation in Results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors argue that the deep learning model is more sensitive to CHD diagnosis than the cardiologists. This is only showing one side of the story (i.e., does the increase in sensitivity come at a cost of lower specificity), and is therefore incomplete. A standard NRI analysis would be more customary and balanced.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors reorganized cardiologist comparison using NRI metric across 10 randomly sampled test groups; in round 2 added NRI(+) and NRI(-) components as suggested.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors should consider displaying precision-recall curves in addition to ROC.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added precision-recall curves to Fig.1 and PR-AUC values to supplementary tables, noting label imbalance considerations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proportion of tracings excluded for 'corruption' is very high (40% in Ref A and 50% in Ref B). This is concerning, and may be a source of bias. More detail is needed regarding assessment of tracing quality and criteria for excluding tracings based on noise. Ideally an objective definition would be applied.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified definition: ECG data with >20% signal amplitudes exceeding 5 mV or >20% recorded values of 0; clarified that signal corruption is common in pediatric ECG; revised Methods to make exclusion criteria explicit and unrelated to CHD status.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors argue that a potential value of the CHDdECG model is better detection of CHD in resource-poor settings, but the model was not evaluated in such settings (i.e., it was evaluated in two large tertiary care centers). I would also acknowledge geographic specificity of train/test as a potential limitation to generalizability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a sentence about geographic and temporal specificity as a limitation; in round 2 added a third external validation cohort from Northeast China (Center-C, ~2300 km away, different ECG device brand).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For data pre-processing, the authors normalized the three types of features using z-score. However, this approach will eliminate true amplitude for QRS-complex, which is the supportive evidence for some morphology anomaly. The authors should provide the reason for ignoring the amplitude information.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors justified z-score normalization for stable DL training, argued absolute amplitudes were linearly scaled and that DL models extract patterns rather than rely on raw amplitude; expert reviewers noted preferred handling.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please add ablation study for utilizing Xe, Xw and Xc as feature input separately. And the authors should discuss the effectiveness and rationality of using the three feature extraction methods according to the ablation results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added an ablation study (Fig. S1) comparing single and combined feature modalities (ECG signal, clinical, wavelet); showed all-three combination outperforms individual modalities, particularly on recall.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although I agree the disease labels used in this study are likely of good quality, I would nevertheless acknowledge the possibility of label misclassification as a limitation. As the authors argue, CHD can be present with ECG abnormalities below the level of human detection, and since many patients were included after having ECGs performed for non-cardiac indications, it is possible that some of these patients labeled as non-CHD actually had CHD that was never diagnosed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added label misclassification as a stated limitation in the Discussion section, noting the need for a prospective protocol with standardized diagnostic workup for all individuals.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A more precise external validation is necessary. I suggest obtaining and using external validation data from another country or a different device company. Alongside AUROC, the authors should also describe the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acquired an additional external test set from Northeast China (Center-C, 2300 km from Guangzhou) with a different ECG device brand (NIHON KOHDEN ECG-2550 vs GE MAC800); added AUROC and PR-AUC across all three test sets.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I would like the authors to verify whether any patients from the external validation data set were included in the training data set. If so, how can this be ensured?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors excluded Center-B patients already present in Center-A using the enterprise master patient index (EMPI) with age, date of birth, sex, and name; for Center-C, used spatial distance and patient-info comparison to ensure non-overlap. Clarification added to Methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors are requested to elucidate the process of model structure selection and the training process for the final model. Can the authors affirm with certainty that, among various models or structures considered, the final model selected is indeed the most accurate? Furthermore, should the deep learning model using waves prove to be more advanced, the necessity of employing wavelets of clinical features may be eliminated. In this context, the authors need to ponder whether such a process could lead to overfitting accuracy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors detailed model structure selection process: ablation study (Fig S1), comparison with classical models (CNN, LSTM, kNN, XGBoost, RF) in Tables S3-S4, and justified wavelet branch with information-preference references; argued strong external test performance suggests against overfitting.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The developed model's accuracy should be checked further in terms of stratification by patient age, sex, and heart rate. Additionally, the authors should provide a baseline characteristics table for the patient cohort.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added stratified performance analysis (Table S5) by sex, age, and heart rate across all three cohorts, with ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Spec, Sens, Brier; added baseline characteristics in Table S2.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Three reviewers across 2 review rounds (Rev #1 + #2 in R1, Rev #1 + #3 in R2; Rev #2 not in R2). Round 3 R1 and R3 both confirmed acceptance. Strong methodological revision trajectory.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It appears the goal was to predict underlying left ventricular pathology (subclinical or concealed) prior to initiation or chemotherapy. Given CTRCD is believed to be caused by the chemotherapeutic regimen, it seems unlikely that we will be able to predict this future event before the inciting factor is actually introduced. It brings up the question of - what is the model actually predicting? I suspect the AI-EF model likely just predicts an overall poor LV substrate and susceptibility to any adverse exposures and as such is not necessarily specific for CTRCD.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the model detects baseline cardiac abnormalities determining susceptibility to cardiotoxic agents (not CTRCD per se); revised abstract, discussion, and conclusions; built new AI-CTRCD model via transfer learning specifically trained on patients receiving anthracyclines.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Did the authors consider just using the model to detect the presence of CTRCD once it develops? ECGs taken after the initiation of chemotherapy could contain information about the damage caused specifically by the chemotherapy and thus could improve the prediction.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors evaluated post-chemotherapy ECGs in 787 patients and found AI-EF score still stratified CTRCD risk (HR 2.64); acknowledged selection bias in post-chemo ECGs (symptomatic patients) and added clarification in Discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the specific prediction of CTRCD, perhaps the authors might need to consider training and evaluating a new model among patients who have actually begun chemotherapy. I realize the authors have pointed out a limitation related to sample size with doing this, but perhaps their ability to successfully collaborate with multiple institutions based on their publication regarding the AI-EF model derivation (ref 26) and potential use of generative adversarial networks could help address the limited sample size.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors collaborated with Keio University Hospital (Japan) to add 190 chemotherapy patients; retrained the AI-EF model via transfer learning specifically for CTRCD prediction (AI-CTRCD model); revised tables and figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The AUC of 0.77 vs. 0.75 seems to be a marginal improvement in performance with addition of the AI-EF to model to known risk factors. Although this difference was shown to be statistically significant, one can argue that it might not necessarily be clinically important. The clinical risk factors model appears to do well on its own (AUV 0.75). Can the authors provide an AUC for the AI-EF model by itself to see if using the ECG alone would be sufficient for prediction if other clinical variables/risk factors are not readily available.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added AUROC for AI-CTRCD alone (0.672), a 4-variable model with AI (0.750), and deployment simulation showing detection of 32 additional CTRCD cases at fixed echo capacity; rephrased significance language throughout.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the results section, the authors mention that 1,138 individuals were enrolled. Were these patients prospectively enrolled or did the authors simply mean that data on these patients were extracted from electronic health records? If the latter, would suggest re-wording to avoid confusion.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 1,138 individuals were retrospectively identified from MGB EDW, not prospectively enrolled; updated wording in Results and Methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors state that the 'AI-EF model demonstrated excellent stratification of the risk of CRTCD' and I was wondering how this was determined? Based on the hazard ratio? an AUC of 0.77, a positive predictive value of 16.9%? I would not consider any of these 'excellent stratification' and this sentence seems overstated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors rephrased 'excellent stratification' to 'The AI-CTRCD model stratified the baseline risk of CTRCD using ECG.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When evaluating the performance of the AI-EF model, did the authors make sure that the patients included in the cohort presented in this manuscript were not included in the original training and validation cohorts given their prior paper (ref 26) discussing model derivation mentions that data was obtained from BWH, MGH, UCSF, and Keio.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors found a minor overlap; developed a new AI-EF model excluding the study population ECGs from training, demonstrated equivalent AUROC (0.91 BWH; 0.89 MGH; 0.91 UCSF; 0.92 Keio); used the new model for transfer learning.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Did the authors consider sex-based stratification when evaluating the performance of the 2 models described given, we know that there are sex-based differences in cardiovascular outcomes?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sex-stratified subgroup analysis (Fig 3C, 3D): male HR 2.54 (95%CI 1.41-4.58), female HR 2.70 (95%CI 1.43-5.12); both significant.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: 7.1% in the low AI-EF score group developed anthracycline-related cardiomyopathy vs. 8.9% overall and 12.9% in the high AI-EF score group; alternatively expressed, 41 of the 99 patients who developed anthracycline-related cardiomyopathy had a low-risk score. While the hazard model appears promising, the prognostic performance, the differential ability to stratify into truly low risk and truly high risk by the AI-ECG algorithm for low EF does not seem to be as strong.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors re-calculated with new AI-CTRCD model: HR 2.66, incidence rate 8.94 vs 3.09 per 100 person-years; using full model with clinical variables, ~7-fold risk difference, and explained model is meant to be used with clinical variables in a combined prediction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Retrospective datasets always pose a challenge; how many of the patients did have a pre- and post-therapy echocardiogram or EF assessment that would allow for robust adjudication of primary event rate?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors found 581 patients (57.5%) had both pre- and post-therapy LVEF assessment; HR 2.43 still observed; added analysis and limitations in Discussion noting potential bias from missing follow-up echos.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the reporting of the anthracycline dose, cumulative doxorubicin equivalents is the most commonly reported and might be worth changing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added cumulative doxorubicin equivalents reporting; ran additional Cox analysis using cumulative dose (HR 1.97 [1.24-3.12]); justified using initial dose for prediction (cumulative dose not available at chemo start); added stratified analysis by cumulative dose subgroups.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Round 2 added Reviewer #3 with only minor reference-update concerns. Major leakage/overlap concern (C07) from R1 was addressed with model rebuild. C04 deployment simulation is a notable strength.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It was not entirely clear if the revision addressed the prior reviewer comments about whether multiple repeat prompts were attempted to asses for consistency in ChatGPT ADA's behavior and choices of analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed multiple repeat prompts in different chat sessions consistently produced the same ML model and parameter selections, with one exception under compute constraints; revised Discussion to clarify consistency assessment and lack of hallucinations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The revision could benefit from a sharper description of the previous reviewer's comments between the well-curated (trial) datasets used for testing compared to the real-world clinical data sources that are likely to have much more missingness and irregularities. Half the battle in clinical machine learning projects is typically the data pre-processing to get heterogeneous clinical data in irregular data formats into a well-structured data frame to enable the AutoML process.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised Limitations section to explicitly acknowledge gap between well-curated trial datasets and real-world clinical data, noting more advanced preprocessing would be needed and ChatGPT ADA's effectiveness in that setting remains to be assessed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: As a more general presentation comment, many of the chat interaction screenshots (e.g. Figure 2) appear illegible at lower resolution when formatted into PDF. These need to be high resolution in publication, or better yet, consider simply including the text of the chat logs (as in the Supplementary material chat logs). These are essential to the value of this manuscript, as they provide the blueprint for readers to replicate the process in their own studies.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors converted all interactions to text format (Supplementary Notes 1-4), revised Fig.2 to include only key parts at higher resolution; removed redundant Supplementary Fig.1.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: PDF includes editorial note that manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal; only revision-round comments included. Only 1 round of Nature Comm review. Rev #1 had a minor SHAP contextualization comment (resolved); Rev #3 had no remarks. The 3 substantive concerns are from Rev #2's second-pass evaluation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The experiments were conducted on two datasets, one of which (Multi-Domain Sentiment) is a general domain dataset that does not relate to clinical data. Further, the second dataset is constructed based on assumptions that do not guarantee the presence of 'in the wild' or 'distribution-shift' scenarios. The experimental evidence does not seem to be sufficient to make such claims. I would recommend using publicly available domain-shift datasets to validate the proposed solution, without being limited to NLP-only datasets.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added experiments on Stanford diverse dermatology images (DDI) dataset with documented distribution shift, and in round 2 added Camelyon17-WILDS histopathology benchmark. Showed SUDO correlates with model performance across modalities.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proposed solution (SUDO) is explained in plain language as an algorithm; however, I find there is a lack of motivation and critical reasoning regarding potential corner cases where this algorithm could fail. For instance, the authors mention that deep neural nets can make class posterior predictions with very high confidence and still fail, which could render the inference probability estimates collected on 'in-the-wild' samples less meaningful. Therefore, the study requires more theoretical justification, along with additional experimental analysis, to support the claims made.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors conducted simulated-data stress tests varying distribution shift, class imbalance, third-class injection, and label noise. Showed SUDO continues to correlate with model performance in most scenarios but fails with drastic label noise or class-distribution flip; added 'Exploring the limits of SUDO with simulated data' section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although the authors discuss related literature in identifying unreliable AI predictions in the introduction and reverse testing and validation in the conclusion, there are important gaps in the literature review with respect to evaluating model accuracy with scarce or no labeled data. It is necessary to draw connections with these works and characterize the contribution of this paper in light of these developments.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors incorporated suggested references (positive-unlabeled, semi-supervised, verification bias) into Introduction and Discussion; emphasized SUDO's data-centric (not model-centric) positioning and the gap in identifying unreliable predictions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Methods for statistical inference are neither provided nor discussed. For example, one would need procedures for statistical testing and interval estimation to evaluate algorithmic bias and to compare the area under the reliability completeness curve for two candidate models.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors positioned SUDO as upstream of statistical inference (providing ranking and bias flag); added Discussion paragraph that SUDO is one step in decision-making and subsequent statistical tests would be needed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: SUDO relies on several hyperparameter and modeling choices, including the discretion into quantiles, the number of samples from each quantile, the choice of classifier, choice of discrepancy metric and threshold, etc. Can the authors provide more discussion and/or evaluation of the sensitivity of their method to these choices? What specific guidance can be provided to practitioners?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig.4) varying sample count (200 vs 50), classifier (logistic regression vs random forest), and label noise; SUDO correlation remained strong (|p|>0.94). Added Practical Guidelines for using SUDO (page 7).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The MultiSentiment dataset is used to illustrate the utility of SUDO. While I agree with the authors that this dataset is a good testing ground, the paper is motivated by the application of AI in medicine. It would be preferable for this analysis to be supplemental and for a publicly available medical dataset to be presented in the main text. For example, the MIMIC dataset (or potentially the MIMIC phenotype annotation dataset) is one option and well-known by the ML for health community.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors relegated MultiSentiment results to Supplementary and added Stanford DDI dataset to main text; pointed to response to Theme 1.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Will any code for SUDO be made publicly available?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Initially: 'Our code is currently undergoing a patent review and is thus not publicly available.' Round 2 response: Authors decided to open-source SUDO codebase at https://github.com/flatironhealth/SUDO. Code Availability statement updated.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The lack of statistical inference procedures is a major limitation and should at least be pointed out in the discussion section. Although the authors argue one can rank competing models with the reliability-completeness curve, without uncertainty estimates it is impossible to know if these rankings are trustworthy. The same issue arises when evaluating model fairness and in identifying unreliable predictions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed and added to Discussion: SUDO is one of the first steps in decision-making; subsequent statistical significance tests would be needed for trustworthy conclusions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors partially addressed this concern by adding in the Stanford Dermatology dataset, as well as synthetic data, and thereby adding positive results on new datasets and outside the text domain. However, a significantly stronger case would have been made if the authors showed these results on in-the-wild suites/benchmarks (e.g. WILDS, a very popular 10-benchmark dataset including pathology + cell imaging), to take away any possibility of cherrypicking.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Camelyon17-WILDS histopathology benchmark experiment, showing SUDO correlation (p=-0.79) with model performance on hospital-shifted data.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Three review rounds. Rev #1 replaced by Rev #3 in R2 (different person responding to R1's concerns). Paper is methods-oriented (evaluation framework) but uses image+NLP examples; concerns mapped to MLGG dimensions where applicable. Note C04 was first marked resolved=false in initial response but rephrased as 'positioning' rather than addressing; reviewer pushed back in R2 and authors accepted limitation.

OUT_OF_SCOPE: Paper is about gene-signature embeddings (FRoGS) for drug target prediction using L1000 Connectivity Map. This is omics/bioinformatics (GO terms, RNA-seq, shRNA/cDNA perturbations), explicitly excluded from MLGG scope per CLAUDE.md (【omics (TCGA/scRNA/GWAS)】). Reviewer concerns center on biology, gene embedding methodology, and bioinformatics validation rather than clinical retrospective cohort ML.

OUT_OF_SCOPE: Paper is itself a methodological study OF data leakage in connectome-based (neuroimaging/fMRI) ML models. Modality is functional/structural connectivity (neuroimaging), not retrospective EHR/tabular binary classification. MLGG explicitly excludes imaging. The paper IS directly relevant to MLGG's mission philosophically (leakage characterization), and reviewer concerns are mostly minor methodological refinements (z-scoring metric, q^2 negative values, family-leakage analysis depth, code availability) - none meet the 'substantive concern affecting a retrospective EHR binary-classification publication' bar. Recommend referencing this paper in MLGG documentation as a meta-citation rather than extracting per-concern entries.

OUT_OF_SCOPE: Paper develops a cfDNA methylation-based tissue-of-origin classifier for Cancers of Unknown Primary. This is omics (methylation profiling of cell-free DNA), explicitly excluded from MLGG scope (omics tracks Scanpy/limma/PLINK). PDF also notes prior review elsewhere; only two reviewers' Nature Comm round comments included. Concerns focus on lack of gold-standard tissue benchmark, scarcity of CUP tissue, and clinical utility - bioinformatics/oncology-specific, not retrospective EHR ML.

OUT_OF_SCOPE: Paper is histopathologic image-based (whole-slide imaging + multiple instance learning) deep-learning classifier for platinum response in ovarian cancer. Modality is histopathology imaging, explicitly excluded from MLGG (imaging not covered). Reviewer concerns focus on dataset size, MIL methodology, cancer-segmentation model validation, and transcriptomic integration - imaging-specific evaluations outside MLGG's tabular/EHR scope.

OUT_OF_SCOPE: Paper is PhageHostLearn predicting Klebsiella phage-host specificity at strain level using bacterial/phage genomic sequences and protein embeddings. This is microbial genomics, not clinical retrospective cohort ML on patients. Out of MLGG scope (omics/bioinformatics). Reviewer #6 raises an interesting leakage concern about genomic-similarity between train/test (LOGOCV insufficient when groups of very similar strains exist) - methodologically relevant to MLGG's leakage philosophy but the subject domain is microbial genomics, not patient prediction.

OUT_OF_SCOPE: Paper is whole-slide-image deep learning for cervical cytology grading (AICS system, YOLOv3 + Xception + U-Net). Modality is digital pathology/cytology imaging - explicitly excluded from MLGG scope. Reviewer concerns center on patch annotation, scanner/staining variation, color augmentation, HPV co-testing context - imaging-specific QA outside MLGG's retrospective EHR tabular binary classification scope.
